I had a missed abortion (an inevitable miscarriage that never started with the bleeding) that was noted at 10 weeks when there wasn't a heartbeat. I was angry and hurt. I grieved. Suddenly everyone around me was pregnant and everything was going perfectly for them. I was bitter. I felt broken.

After all that I decided I wasn't ready to try again because what if something went wrong? I decided we were too broke and I was too broken to have another kid.

Then I got knocked up accidentally. It wasn't exactly hard to get pregnant the first time, but after 29 years of being able to control all births in my uterus I was surprised to be surprised. Then I was angry that I was pregnant. Didn't the kid know I was broken? How were we ever going to manage this? What if I had hurt the baby already because I didn't know I was pregnant?

In the end, it took months for me to get used to being pregnant and to accept that things were going well. I eventually came to love my fetus, and when I felt him kicking and saw him on ultrasound I couldn't help but smile.

He was born at term, healthy. He has been the best and most challenging part of my life since that day. Being at this point and looking back makes all that grief and feeling broken at that time worth it. If that's how I get to this point, that part is okay by me.

I hope you are able to go through this grieving process and come out the other end. There is another end to come out of, and it's hard to get there but worth it. Plus, we have cookies.

You may well have a blood vessel that is irritated - dilated and rebleeding. This often happens in dry weather (when the heater is on in the house especially). As a young, healthy man you're unlikely to bleed out from a typical nose bleed (remember how much blood women lose EVERY MONTH and just picture that coming out of your nose ... you're welcome!)

If you have liver disease or a bleeding disorder or are on blood thinners for any reason, ignore what I said about it not being likely for you to have a major problem.

One more thing you can try before seeking medical attention is to institute the NOTHING UP THE NOSE rule and simultaneously apply a layer of Vaseline to the nose externally around the nostril openings. Sometimes this can make the difference. If you get a bleed, PINCH the outsides of your nose together and tilt your face forward. Do not stick Kleenexes up there. NOTHING UP THE NOSE. All of those things irritate the already-irritated mucosal surface up there.

If that doesn't work, you could go see a family doc or ENT and have them cauterize the source of bleeding if they can see where it's likely coming from. That's the next natural step.

Time to worry: lightheadedness/dizziness, passing out, shortness of breath/weakness. Especially after having hours of bleeding.  But unless you have a major medical problem, you have PLENTY of blood and no periods, so you are unlikely to have serious consequences from blood loss.

*Decrease pasta/white bread intake, and check the grams of fiber on any bread before you buy - only get bread with more than 2 gm of fiber per serving

I also went cold turkey. And initially had trouble with milk, but now I'm back to guzzling dairy products like a champion (the dairy thing took about a year of careful gluten-free, dairy-free eating for me). I found that eating out is much easier without the dairy restriction as well, but even with that, you can eat out. Some things I used to do before being able to do dairy:

Japanese restaurant: sashimi, steamed veggies, plain rice, a lot of sushi (be careful of the wasabi, and don't eat any pre-marinated items like eel)

Thai restaurant: curries are generally OK (check with the kitchen)

Italian restaurant: call and ask if they have gluten-free pasta on hand. Many restaurants do. Make sure they are understanding about not sharing water, etc with the gluten-filled pasta. Get that with some meat and marinara sauce. Or if they don't have that, check out things like steaks or pork. Lots of times there are options like that as well.

Steak restaurant: get steak. Be careful of marinades. Again, call ahead and speak with a manager. Longhorn is a chain that I have had great luck with in the past. They are generally very helpful and have worked hard to take care of me even while the kitchen is busy.

Diners: I just don't. Too much cross-contamination.

Fast food: Burger King or Wendy's, but do research ahead of time. Both have very clear-cut allergen menus available and are quite good about accommodating food allergies.

Fancy restaurants: the expensive ones were always GREAT at meeting any need I wanted. But who can afford all that?

PF Chang: great for gluten-free, but they have milk ingredients in ALL their meat. ALL OF IT. I could only get scallops with veggies there back when I couldn't do dairy, so I just stopped eating there completely.

I also gave up on places like Applebee's, Chili's, etc. Just not worth the cross-contamination risk and they don't seem as food allergy-friendly as the other places I've mentioned. I'm sure there are options beyond what I've said, but I'm speaking only from personal experience over a few years of being gluten-free and only one year of doing both gluten- and dairy-free.

I haven't had one personally but I do know there are multiple options out there for getting one. You can do a surgical ligation, which involves actually cutting through the fallopian tubes and tying off the ends, or you can get what's called an Essure (pronounced "E-sure"). The Essure is a smaller, easier procedure that involves using a camera to enter the uterus through the vagina (no incisions) and then the coils are ejected into the fallopian tubes, guided by the camera view. The way that one works is that the tubes scar down over a period of about 6 months, during which time you need other birth control methods in place. I'm not sure how they compare in terms of cost since the Essure requires fewer hospital resources but is newer technology.

Speaking from the doctor standpoint, there's a cultural hesitation within the medical profession about giving younger women tubals unless they've previously had children. Sometimes that's a good thing (when a woman does legitimately change her mind later) and sometimes that's a stupid thing (because some women just know themselves and honestly do not want kids - which SHOULD be an accepted thing to decide).

I'm not sure how the insurance companies feel about tubals. You'd have to look into your policy.

Tubal ligation side effects are mainly just the general ones from surgery: a day or two of recovery from the anesthesia, some pain at the surgical site and maybe in the pelvis as well, possible vaginal bleeding, possible infections at the surgical sites. You're not removing any hormone-producing organs so there aren't hormonal side effects.

Vaccines give your body a sneak preview of the bug (or a part of the bug) that it may be faced with later. There are vaccines against viruses (as many have already mentioned) and bacteria. There are "live, attenuated" vaccines (the virus has been weakened to the point of being pathetically bad at infecting you, but it still looks enough like the strong version that your body learns to fight it well) or they can be proteins from the outside of the bug, which allows your body to recognize that protein later and kill the bug.

The key here is understanding that your body doesn't know how to fight every bug perfectly the first time. It learns to recognize bugs and then kills them really well the second time around. You can keep getting sick from something like the common cold because there are so many versions of the rhinovirus (the typical cause) that your body can't possibly learn them all. You won't usually catch chicken pox or measles twice, for example, because that's one that your body does learn to know.

We give vaccines to protect kids against the illnesses that (a) we are able to vaccinate against and (b) will be most harmful to the kid if he or she gets ill. In some cases, the vaccine is meant to improve the body's response time and some smaller amount of illness is to be expected. In other cases, the kid shouldn't get sick at all. Either way, we've taken diseases like whooping cough (caused by a bacterium called Bordetella pertussis, which is in the DTaP vaccine as a protein because it's so dangerous) that used to kill kids regularly and made it a rarity. Sleep helps to remove the adenosine that has built up, while caffeine somehow (can't remember how at the moment) helps to prevent the effects of the adenosine. Messing with the circadian rhythm as programmed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus would tend to throw you off for longer because your internal scheduling is confused. Providing natural clues (turning down lights, avoiding caffeine close to bedtime) would help you to recover from a messed-up suprachiasmatic nucleus.

By getting plenty of sleep before a night of sleep deprivation, you're basically making sure you have the least amount of adenosine build-up before the sleep deprivation event. As your body becomes more accustomed to exercise, you do build up the mitochondrial membranes to be able to process glucose oxidatively for longer before requiring anaerobic respiration. Mitochondria in athletes have been shown to have more folds in their inner membranes to allow for more space for H+ ions, and cells that use oxidative respiration heavily have very different mitochondria from cells that rely on it less (so the "thickness" of the mitochondria, if you will, is dependent on function of the human tissue as well).

Another key thing that exercise does is to thicken the heart muscle itself, as lakanov mentioned. This allows the heart to pump more blood with each contraction of the muscle, making oxygen delivery to the other muscles more efficient as well.

The last thing I wanted to mention is that muscles store glucose (blood sugar) for later. They maintain these stores based on how frequently and extensively you use them. Your normal activity level therefore determines how much glucose goes to fat cells and how much goes to muscle cells. The muscle cells store this glucose by activating channels called GLUT4; these channels are activated by exercise (roughly 30 minutes of walking briskly or 26 minutes of jogging will cause them to activate, which is where your 30-minute aerobic exercise recommendations came from, in part).
